director.chapterArc: A procedural and emotional transition from surgical delay to the final separation of brotherhood, marked by a momentary spiritual failure followed by human connection.
director.restraintNote: Maintain clinical precision for Doctor Keel; allow Jab's internal monologue regarding his power to feel hollow rather than magical. The scene with Wyck requires dry humor without breaking character voices. End on the quiet finality of separation, not melodrama.

cues.delivery: Clinical observation. Jab's perspective on the doctor is one of wary recognition.
cues.from: Doctor Keel came at the tenth hour and she was shorter and worse, exactly as advertised.
cues.through: She was a tall woman of about forty-five with her sleeves rolled past the elbow and forearms like a person who rowed, and she came down the ward, looked at the leg for eleven seconds, put two fingers on the boy's foot, watched the toes, and then turned round and said to Jab:
cues.reason: Establishes Doctor Keel as a figure of authority and competence.

cues.delivery: Fast, flat delivery for dialogue. No apology in the voice.
cues.through: "I know what he is. I've read it and I've looked at it and I'm going to look at a picture of the inside of it in about an hour." She said it fast and flat and without any apology in it whatsoever. "Here's the reason, and it's the only one you're getting, and it's a good one. If I open that leg today I'm opening it on a child who has had one bag of fluid and eight hours of medicine after seven weeks of being dried out on a road. If I open it tomorrow morning I'm opening it on a child who's had a day of both, and he'll be on the table for two hours either way, and the second one comes off the table better."
cues.reason: Reflects Keel's efficiency and lack of time.

cues.delivery: Flat delivery for the statistic about the amputation. Jab's silence is heavy.
cues.from: "Six were straightforwardly all right. Two took a second go and were all right after that. One I took the leg off at the knee." Doctor Keel did not look away while she said it. "He's twelve now and he's a perfectly ordinary boy and he is extremely rude about my handwriting, and I'd have him in here tomorrow to talk to you if this were the kind of station where that was allowed, and it isn't, so you'll have to take my word for him."
cues.through: "Good," said Doctor Keel. "Now go and eat something, because you are grey, and I do not operate on children whose people fall over in my corridor."
cues.reason: The reality of the surgery must land without melodrama.

cues.delivery: Sensory focus on the metal. A moment of quiet recognition.
cues.from: He had not known it was that colour. It had been grey going green with four years of skin and smoke and river on it, and what came out of the bin was pale and clean and dull, smooth as an egg on one face and dimpled on the other, and it caught the flat white light off the ceiling in a way it had never once caught firelight. It looked like a thing off a bar. It looked exactly like the thing it had been before anybody picked it up.
cues.through: He kept the tag. He did not know why. He put it in his coat pocket with his thumb over the number.
cues.reason: The return of the artifact is a physical and emotional anchor.

cues.delivery: Instructional tone for the warning about metal.
cues.reason: Establishes the physical rules of the machine room.

cues.delivery: Jab's voice is level but strained. Tonk's questions are factual.
cues.from: "Will they mend my leg," said Tonk, from the bed, out of nowhere, in a small clear voice.
cues.through: "I know," said Jab, and made himself keep his voice level and keep looking at him. "I'm not going to tell you they made me. I'm standing here on my own feet and I'm going to let go of your hand, because that machine would take the metal off my neck and fire it across the room, and there's a four-year-old going into that room."
cues.reason: The separation of the brother requires a calm facade.

cues.delivery: Internal monologue. The silence is heavy and the failure of power feels physical.
cues.from: He sat on it with a paper tray in his lap holding a thumb-length of river metal on a cord, and the heavy door shut with a sound like a lid, and then, from behind a wall as thick as a bank, the knocking started.
cues.through: Nothing at all. Not up, not down, not a slope in the dark, not the smallest lean in any direction. There was the concrete and the knocking and the cold, and there was a boy sitting on a bench with an empty space behind his ribs where something used to be.
cues.reason: Jab's spiritual void must be felt as a loss.

cues.delivery: Dessa speaks with flat certainty. Jab's confession is raw but controlled.
cues.from: "On his back," she said. "He hasn't moved. There's two of them in the room with him and they're at the far side, and one of them is sitting down." She paused. "He hasn't moved at all. He's very good at it."
cues.through: "I know," said Dessa. "You counted the paces last night. Out loud. All three hundred and forty of them."
cues.reason: The exchange of power types needs to feel like a shared reality.

cues.delivery: Tonk's outrage is factual. Wyck's presence is solid and unyielding.
cues.from: "It knocked like a man," said Tonk, with the outrage of a person who has been personally imposed upon, "mending a roof, inside my leg," and Jab laughed, and put the cord back over his head, and walked beside the rolling bed all the way up the slope.
cues.through: "Wyck," said the big boy, to Jab, as an afterthought, and pulled the chair round with his foot and sat down on it backward with the bar across his knees, and stayed for an hour and a half.
cues.reason: The interaction with the injured boy grounds the scene.

cues.delivery: Wyck's dialogue is dry and direct. Jab's laughter is a release of tension.
cues.from: "That's going to hurt worse tomorrow than it does now."
cues.through: "Do it again," said Tonk, delighted and appalled, in exactly the voice he had used about a squirrel, and Jab put his head down on the edge of the bed and laughed until his ribs hurt.
cues.reason: The humor must be subtle to fit the tone.

cues.delivery: Katori's observation is sharp and specific. Jab's silence acknowledges the truth.
cues.from: "No," said Katori, "you're not. That's why I said the eighth hour and not tomorrow afternoon." She stood there. "I'm going to say one thing and then I'll go. The nurse at the desk told me what you had in your coat when you came through the gate. Three twists of bark, in paper, folded in eights."
cues.through: She went to the door and stopped.
cues.reason: The recognition of his sacrifice must be felt.

cues.delivery: Callie's warning is delivered with flat precision.
cues.from: "There's a thing in my mother's head they can't take out," she said, in the flat way a person says a thing they have decided to say the same way every time. "They can make her days better and they can't make more of them, and she takes pills at the eighth hour every morning in this building, and if she's not within a mile of it she doesn't get them. So we're here." She turned the tag on her own wrist over. "Four hundred miles, on a wagon, to get her to a door. And then we got to the door and everything on the other side of it turned out to be a different problem."
cues.reason: The future threat must be stated as a fact.

cues.delivery: Final separation. Jab's voice is steady but the action of letting go is heavy.
cues.from: They had taken the bag off the hook and there was a nurse doing something with a chart and Doctor Keel was standing at the foot of the bed with her sleeves already rolled, saying something to Tonk that made him look extremely suspicious.
cues.reason: The end of the chapter requires a quiet resolution.

pauses.before: Because I've got something and it doesn't reach past my own arm

pauses.after: They brought Tonk out at the end of it with his eyes shut and his hair every which way, and he opened them as they crossed the yellow line and found Jab standing there with a paper tray in his hands.
pauses.reason: Speaker reset and shift to Tonk's observation.

pauses.after: "Forty is what you'd count out for a road like that. Forty, at two a day. And you came in on the sixteenth day with three left, which means you've been halving them for a week, which means somebody sat down at a fire every night for a week and did a sum about his own brother's pain, and then did the sum again in the morning." She was looking out of the window over the bed. "I'm not going to say anything else about it. I only wanted you to know that somebody in this station has done the sum backwards and knows what's in it."
pauses.reason: Pause for Katori's observation of Jab's sacrifice.

pauses.reason: Emphasis on the arithmetic of survival.

pauses.after: "That's the bit nobody warns you about. The road's the hard part right up until you finish it." She looked at him sideways. "I was quite good at the road."
pauses.reason: Completed thought on the road comparison.

pauses.after: The fish went with him. It was wood, and wood did not matter to anything, and Doctor Keel looked at it and said it could go as far as the door and would be waiting at the other end, and then looked at the boy's face and changed her mind out loud, in front of everybody, and said that it could go the whole way and she would put it in his hand herself when he was asleep.
pauses.reason: Speaker reset and shift to Tonk's request for the fish.
